{{Short description|Mathematical object}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Kodaira–Spencer map''', introduced by [[Kunihiko Kodaira]] and [[Donald C. Spencer]], is a [[Map (mathematics)|map]] associated to a [[Deformation theory|deformation]] of a [[Scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] or [[complex manifold]] ''X'', taking a [[tangent space]] of a point of the [[deformation space]] to the first [[cohomology group]] of the [[sheaf (mathematics)|sheaf]] of [[vector field]]s on&nbsp;''X''.

== Definition ==

=== Historical motivation ===
The Kodaira–Spencer map was originally constructed in the setting of complex manifolds. Given a complex [[analytic manifold]] <math>M</math> with charts <math>U_i</math> and biholomorphic maps <math>f_{jk}</math> sending <math>z_k \to z_j = (z_j^1,\ldots, z_j^n)</math> gluing the charts together, the idea of deformation theory is to replace these transition maps <math>f_{jk}(z_k)</math> by parametrized transition maps <math>f_{jk}(z_k, t_1,\ldots, t_k)</math> over some base <math>B</math> (which could be a real manifold) with coordinates <math>t_1,\ldots, t_k</math>, such that <math>f_{jk}(z_k, 0,\ldots, 0) = f_{jk}(z_k)</math>. This means the parameters <math>t_i</math> deform the complex structure of the original complex manifold <math>M</math>. Then, these functions must also satisfy a cocycle condition, which gives a 1-cocycle on <math>M</math> with values in its [[tangent bundle]]. Since the base can be assumed to be a polydisk, this process gives a map between the tangent space of the base to <math>H^1(M, T_M)</math> called the Kodaira–Spencer map.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Kodaira|title=Complex Manifolds and Deformation of Complex Structures|url=https://archive.org/details/complexmanifolds00koda_517|url-access=limited|series=Classics in Mathematics|year=2005|isbn=978-3-540-22614-7|pages=[https://archive.org/details/complexmanifolds00koda_517/page/n190 182]–184, 188–189|doi=10.1007/b138372}}</ref>

=== Original definition ===
More formally, the '''Kodaira–Spencer map''' is<ref>{{harvnb|Huybrechts|2005|loc=6.2.6.}}</ref>

:<math>KS: T_0 B \to H^1(M, T_M)</math>

where
*<math>\mathcal{M} \to B</math> is a smooth [[proper map]] between [[complex space (algebraic geometry)|complex space]]s<ref>The main difference between a complex manifold and a complex space is that the latter is allowed to have a nilpotent.</ref> (i.e., a deformation of the [[special fiber]] <math>M = \mathcal{M}_0</math>.)
*<math>KS</math> is the connecting homomorphism obtained by taking a long exact cohomology sequence of the surjection <math>T \mathcal{M}|_M \to T_0 B \otimes \mathcal{O}_M</math> whose kernel is the tangent bundle <math>T_M</math>.

If <math>v</math> is in <math>T_0B</math>, then its image <math>KS(v)</math> is called the '''Kodaira–Spencer class''' of <math>v</math>.

=== Remarks ===
Because deformation theory has been extended to multiple other contexts, such as deformations in scheme theory, or [[ringed topos|ringed topoi]], there are constructions of the Kodaira–Spencer map for these contexts.

In the scheme theory over a base field <math>k</math> of characteristic <math>0</math>, there is a natural [[bijection]] between isomorphisms classes of <math>\mathcal{X} \to S = \operatorname{Spec}(k[t]/t^2)</math> and <math>H^1(X, TX)</math>.

== Constructions ==

=== Using infinitesimals ===

==== Cocycle condition for deformations ====
Over characteristic <math>0</math> the construction of the Kodaira–Spencer map<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Arbarello|author-link1=Enrico Arbarello|url=https://www.springer.com/gp/book/9783540426882|title=Geometry of Algebraic Curves II|last2=Cornalba|author-link2=Maurizio Cornalba|last3=Griffiths|author-link3=Phillip Griffiths|series=Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften|publisher=Springer|year=2011|isbn=9783540426882|pages=172–174}}</ref> can be done using an [[infinitesimal]] interpretation of the cocycle condition. If we have a complex manifold <math>X</math> covered by finitely many charts <math>\mathcal{U} = \{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in I}</math> with coordinates <math>z_\alpha = (z_\alpha^1, \ldots, z_\alpha^n)</math> and transition functions <blockquote><math>f_{\beta\alpha}:U_\beta|_{U_{\alpha\beta}} \to U_\alpha|_{U_{\alpha\beta}}</math> where <math>f_{\alpha\beta}(z_\beta) = z_\alpha</math></blockquote>Recall that a deformation is given by a [[commutative diagram]]<blockquote><math>\begin{matrix}
X & \to & \mathfrak{X} \\
\downarrow & & \downarrow \\
\text{Spec}(\mathbb{C}) & \to & \text{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon])
\end{matrix}</math></blockquote>where <math>\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]</math> is the [[ring of dual numbers]] and the vertical maps are flat, the deformation has the cohomological interpretation as cocycles <math>\tilde{f}_{\alpha\beta}(z_\beta,\varepsilon)</math> on <math>U_\alpha\times \text{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon])</math> where<blockquote><math>z_\alpha = \tilde{f}_{\alpha\beta}(z_\beta,\varepsilon) = f_{\alpha\beta}(z_\beta) + \varepsilon b_{\alpha\beta}(z_\beta)</math></blockquote>If the <math>\tilde{f}_{\alpha\beta}</math> satisfy the cocycle condition, then they glue to the deformation <math>\mathfrak{X}</math>. This can be read as<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
\tilde{f}_{\alpha\gamma}(z_\gamma,\varepsilon) ={}&\tilde{f}_{\alpha\beta}(\tilde{f}_{\beta\gamma}(z_\gamma,\varepsilon),\varepsilon) \\
={}& f_{\alpha\beta}(f_{\beta\gamma}(z_\gamma) + \varepsilon b_{\beta\gamma}(z_\gamma))\\
&+ \varepsilon b_{\alpha\beta}(f_{\beta\gamma}(z_\gamma) + \varepsilon b_{\beta\gamma}(z_\gamma))
\end{align}</math></blockquote>Using the properties of the dual numbers, namely <math>g(a + b\varepsilon) = g(a) + \varepsilon g'(a)b</math>, we have<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
f_{\alpha\beta}(f_{\beta\gamma}(z_\gamma) + \varepsilon b_{\beta\gamma}(z_\gamma)) &= f_{\alpha\beta}(f_{\beta\gamma}(z_\gamma)) + \varepsilon \frac{\partial f_{\alpha\beta}}{\partial z_\beta}(z_\beta)b_{\beta\gamma}(z_\gamma) \\

\end{align}</math></blockquote>and<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
\varepsilon b_{\alpha\beta}(f_{\beta\gamma}(z_\gamma) + \varepsilon b_{\beta\gamma}(z_\gamma)) = \varepsilon b_{\alpha\beta}(z_\beta)
\end{align}</math></blockquote>hence the cocycle condition on <math>U_\alpha\times \text{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon])</math> is the following two rules

# <math>b_{\alpha\gamma} = \frac{\partial f_{\alpha\beta}}{\partial z_\beta}b_{\beta\gamma} + b_{\alpha\beta}</math>
# <math>f_{\alpha\gamma} = f_{\alpha\beta} \circ f_{\beta\gamma}</math>

==== Conversion to cocycles of vector fields ====
The cocycle of the deformation can easily be converted to a cocycle of vector fields <math>\theta = \{\theta_{\alpha\beta} \} \in C^1(\mathcal{U},T_X)</math> as follows: given the cocycle <math>\tilde{f}_{\alpha\beta} = f_{\alpha\beta} + \varepsilon b_{\alpha\beta}</math> we can form the vector field<blockquote><math>\theta_{\alpha\beta} = \sum_{i=1}^n b_{\alpha\beta}^i\frac{\partial}{\partial z_\alpha^i}</math></blockquote>which is a 1-cochain. Then the rule for the transition maps of <math>b_{\alpha\gamma}</math> gives this 1-cochain as a 1-cocycle, hence a class <math>[\theta] \in H^1(X,T_X)</math>.

=== Using vector fields ===
One of the original constructions of this map used vector fields in the settings of [[differential geometry]] and [[complex analysis]].<ref name=":0" /> Given the notation above, the transition from a deformation to the cocycle condition is transparent over a small base of dimension one, so there is only one parameter <math>t</math>. Then, the cocycle condition can be read as<blockquote><math>f^{\alpha}_{ik}(z_k,t) = f_{ij}^{\alpha}(f^1_{kj}(z_k,t), \ldots, f^n_{kj}(z_k,t),t)</math></blockquote>Then, the derivative of <math>f^{\alpha}_{ik}(z_k,t)</math> with respect to <math>t</math> can be calculated from the previous equation as<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
\frac{\partial f^{\alpha}_{ik}(z_k,t)}{\partial t} &= \frac{\partial f^{\alpha}_{ij}(z_j,t)}{\partial t}
 + \sum^n_{\beta = 0} \frac{\partial f^{\alpha}_{ij}(z_j,t)}{\partial f_{jk}^\beta(z_k,t)}\cdot
 \frac{\partial f^{\beta}_{jk}(z_k,t)}{\partial t} \\
\end{align}</math></blockquote>Note because <math>z_j^\beta = f_{jk}^\beta(z_k,t)</math> and <math>z_i^\alpha = f_{ij}^{\alpha}(z_j,t)</math>, then the derivative reads as <blockquote><math>\begin{align}
\frac{\partial f^{\alpha}_{ik}(z_k,t)}{\partial t} &= \frac{\partial f^{\alpha}_{ij}(z_j,t)}{\partial t}
 + \sum^n_{\beta = 0} \frac{\partial z^{\alpha}_i}{\partial z_j^\beta}\cdot
 \frac{\partial f^{\beta}_{jk}(z_k,t)}{\partial t} \\
\end{align}</math></blockquote>With a change of coordinates of the part of the previous holomorphic vector field having these partial derivatives as the coefficients, we can write<blockquote><math>\frac{\partial}{\partial z_j^\beta} = \sum_{\alpha = 1}^n
\frac{
    \partial z_i^\alpha
}{
    \partial z_j^\beta
}\cdot \frac{
    \partial
}{
    \partial z_i^\alpha
}</math></blockquote>Hence we can write up the equation above as the following equation of vector fields<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
\sum_{\alpha=0}^n \frac{\partial f^{\alpha}_{ik}(z_k,t)}{\partial t} \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i^\alpha} =&
\sum_{\alpha=0}^n \frac{\partial f^{\alpha}_{ij}(z_j,t)}{\partial t} \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i^\alpha}
\\& + \sum^n_{\beta = 0}
 \frac{\partial f^{\beta}_{jk}(z_k,t)}{\partial t}  \frac{\partial}{\partial z_j^\beta}  \\
\end{align}</math></blockquote>Rewriting this as the vector fields<blockquote><math>\theta_{ik}(t) = \theta_{ij}(t) + \theta_{jk}(t)</math></blockquote>where<blockquote><math>\theta_{ij}(t) = \frac{\partial f^{\alpha}_{ij}(z_j,t)}{\partial t} \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i^\alpha} </math></blockquote>gives the cocycle condition. Hence <math>\theta_{ij}</math> has an associated class in <math>[\theta_{ij}] \in H^1(M,T_M)</math> from the original deformation <math>\tilde{f}_{ij}</math> of <math>f_{ij}</math>.

=== In scheme theory ===
Deformations of a smooth variety<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.mat.uniroma3.it/users/sernesi/sernesioverviewdefth.pdf|title=An overview of classical deformation theory|last=Sernesi|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200427180649/http://www.mat.uniroma3.it/users/sernesi/sernesioverviewdefth.pdf|archive-date=2020-04-27}}</ref><blockquote><math>\begin{matrix}
X & \to & \mathfrak{X} \\
\downarrow & & \downarrow \\
\text{Spec}(k) & \to & \text{Spec}(k[\varepsilon])
\end{matrix}</math></blockquote>have a Kodaira-Spencer class constructed cohomologically. Associated to this deformation is the short exact sequence<blockquote><math>0 \to \pi^*\Omega^1_{\text{Spec}(k[\varepsilon])} \to \Omega_{\mathfrak{X}}^1 \to \Omega_{\mathfrak{X}/S}^1 \to 0</math></blockquote>(where <math>\pi:\mathfrak{X} \to S = \text{Spec}(k[\varepsilon])</math>) which when tensored by the <math>\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{X}}</math>-module <math>\mathcal{O}_X</math> gives the short exact sequence<blockquote><math>0 \to \mathcal{O}_X \to \Omega^1_{\mathfrak{X}}\otimes\mathcal{O}_X \to \Omega_X^1 \to 0</math></blockquote>Using [[derived categories]], this defines an element in<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
\mathbf{R}\text{Hom}(\Omega_X^1,\mathcal{O}_X[+1]) &\cong
    \mathbf{R}\text{Hom}(\mathcal{O}_X,T_X[+1]) \\
&\cong \text{Ext}^1(\mathcal{O}_X,T_X) \\
&\cong H^1(X,T_X)
\end{align}</math></blockquote>generalizing the Kodaira–Spencer map. Notice this could be generalized to any smooth map <math>f:X \to Y</math> in <math>\text{Sch}/S</math> using the cotangent sequence, giving an element in <math>H^1(X,T_{X/Y}\otimes f^*(\Omega^1_{Y/Z}))</math>.

=== Of ringed topoi ===
One of the most abstract constructions of the Kodaira–Spencer maps comes from the [[cotangent complex]]es associated to a composition of maps of [[Ringed topos|ringed topoi]]<blockquote><math>X \xrightarrow{f} Y \to Z</math></blockquote>Then, associated to this composition is a [[distinguished triangle]]<blockquote><math>f^*\mathbf{L}_{Y/Z} \to \mathbf{L}_{X/Z} \to  \mathbf{L}_{X/Y} \xrightarrow{[+1]}</math></blockquote>and this boundary map forms the Kodaira–Spencer map<ref>{{Cite book|last=Illusie|first=L.|author-link=Luc Illusie|url=http://sites.mathdoc.fr/PMO/PDF/I_ILLUSIE-64.pdf|title=Complexe cotangent ; application a la theorie des deformations|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201125154916/http://sites.mathdoc.fr/PMO/PDF/I_ILLUSIE-64.pdf|access-date=2020-04-27|archive-date=2020-11-25|url-status=dead}}</ref> (or cohomology class, denoted <math>K(X/Y/Z)</math>). If the two maps in the composition are smooth maps of schemes, then this class coincides with the class in <math>H^1(X,T_{X/Y}\otimes f^*(\Omega^1_{Y/Z}))</math>.

== Examples ==

=== With analytic germs ===
The Kodaira–Spencer map when considering analytic germs is easily computable using the tangent cohomology in [[Deformation theory#Cohomological Interpretation of deformations|deformation theory]] and its versal deformations.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Palamodov|title=Several Complex Variables IV|chapter=Deformations of Complex Spaces|series=Encyclopaedia of Mathematical Sciences|year=1990|volume=10|isbn=978-3-642-64766-6|pages=138, 130|doi=10.1007/978-3-642-61263-3_3}}</ref> For example, given the germ of a polynomial <math>f(z_1,\ldots, z_n) \in \mathbb{C}\{z_1,\ldots, z_n \} = H</math>, its space of deformations can be given by the module<blockquote><math>T^1 = \frac{H}{df \cdot H^n}</math></blockquote>For example, if <math>f = y^2 - x^3</math> then its versal deformations is given by<blockquote><math>T^1 = \frac{ \mathbb{C}\{ x,y \} }{(y, x^2)}</math></blockquote>hence an arbitrary deformation is given by <math>F(x,y,a_1,a_2) = y^2 - x^3 +a_1 + a_2x</math>. Then for a vector <math>v \in T_0(\mathbb{C}^2)</math>, which has the basis<blockquote><math>\frac{\partial}{\partial a_1}, \frac{\partial}{\partial a_2}</math></blockquote>there the map <math>KS: v \mapsto v(F)</math> sending<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
\phi_1\frac{\partial}{\partial a_1} + \phi_2 \frac{\partial}{\partial a_2} \mapsto & \phi_1\frac{\partial F}{\partial a_1} + \phi_2 \frac{\partial F}{\partial a_2}  \\
& = \phi_1 + \phi_2\cdot x
\end{align}</math></blockquote>

=== On affine hypersurfaces with the cotangent complex ===
For an affine hypersurface <math>i:X_0 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{A}^n \to \text{Spec}(k)</math> over a field <math>k</math> defined by a polynomial <math>f</math>, there is the associated fundamental triangle<blockquote><math>i^*\mathbf{L}_{\mathbb{A}^n/\text{Spec}(k)} \to
\mathbf{L}_{X_0/\text{Spec}(k)} \to
\mathbf{L}_{X_0/\mathbb{A}^n} \xrightarrow{[+1]} </math></blockquote>Then, applying <math>\mathbf{RHom}(-,\mathcal{O}_{X_0})</math> gives the long exact sequence<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
&\textbf{RHom}(i^*\mathbf{L}_{\mathbb{A}^n/\text{Spec}(k)},\mathcal{O}_{X_0}[+1]) \leftarrow
\textbf{RHom}(\mathbf{L}_{X_0/\text{Spec}(k)},\mathcal{O}_{X_0}[+1]) \leftarrow
\textbf{RHom}(\mathbf{L}_{X_0/\mathbb{A}^n},\mathcal{O}_{X_0}[+1]) \\
\leftarrow &\textbf{RHom}(i^*\mathbf{L}_{\mathbb{A}^n/\text{Spec}(k)},\mathcal{O}_{X_0}) \leftarrow
\textbf{RHom}(\mathbf{L}_{X_0/\text{Spec}(k)},\mathcal{O}_{X_0}) \leftarrow
\textbf{RHom}(\mathbf{L}_{X_0/\mathbb{A}^n},\mathcal{O}_{X_0})
\end{align}</math></blockquote>Recall that there is the isomorphism<blockquote><math>\textbf{RHom}(\mathbf{L}_{X_0/\text{Spec}(k)},\mathcal{O}_{X_0}[+1]) \cong \text{Ext}^1(\mathbf{L}_{X_0/\text{Spec}(k)}, \mathcal{O}_{X_0})</math></blockquote>from general theory of derived categories, and the ext group classifies the first-order deformations. Then, through a series of reductions, this group can be computed. First, since <math>\mathbf{L}_{\mathbb{A}^n/\text{Spec}(k)} \cong \Omega^1_{\mathbb{A}^n/\text{Spec}(k)}</math> is a [[free module]], <math>\textbf{RHom}(i^*\mathbf{L}_{\mathbb{A}^n/\text{Spec}(k)},\mathcal{O}_{X_0}[+1]) = 0</math>. Also, because <math>\mathbf{L}_{X_0/\mathbb{A}^n} \cong \mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2[+1] </math>, there are isomorphisms<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
\textbf{RHom}(\mathbf{L}_{X_0/\mathbb{A}^n},\mathcal{O}_{X_0}[+1]) \cong &
\textbf{RHom}(\mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2[+1],\mathcal{O}_{X_0}[+1]) \\
\cong &
\textbf{RHom}(\mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2,\mathcal{O}_{X_0}) \\
\cong &
\text{Ext}^0(\mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2,\mathcal{O}_{X_0}) \\
\cong & 
\text{Hom}(\mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2,\mathcal{O}_{X_0}) \\
\cong & \mathcal{O}_{X_0}
\end{align} </math></blockquote>The last isomorphism comes from the isomorphism <math>\mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2 \cong \mathcal{I} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{A}^n}} \mathcal{O}_{X_0} </math>, and a morphism in<blockquote><math>\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_0}}(\mathcal{I} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{A}^n}} \mathcal{O}_{X_0} ,\mathcal{O}_{X_0}) </math>  send <math>[gf] \mapsto g'g + (f) </math></blockquote>giving the desired isomorphism. From the cotangent sequence<blockquote><math>\frac{(f)}{(f)^2} \xrightarrow{[g] \mapsto dg\otimes 1}
\Omega^1_{\mathbb{A}^n}\otimes \mathcal{O}_{X_0} \to \Omega^1_{X_0/\text{Spec}(k)} \to 0</math></blockquote>(which is a truncated version of the fundamental triangle) the connecting map of the long [[exact sequence]] is the dual of <math>[g] \mapsto dg \otimes 1 </math>, giving the isomorphism<blockquote><math>\text{Ext}^1(\mathbf{L}_{X_0/k}, \mathcal{O}_{X_0}) \cong
\frac{k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]}{
    \left(f, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}, \ldots, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n} \right)
    
} </math></blockquote>Note this computation can be done by using the cotangent sequence and computing <math>\text{Ext}^1(\Omega^1_{X_0},\mathcal{O}_{X_0})</math>.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Talpo|first1=Mattia|last2=Vistoli|first2=Angelo|author-link2=Angelo Vistoli|date=2011-01-30|title=Deformation theory from the point of view of fibered categories|pages=25, exercise 3.25|class=math.AG|eprint=1006.0497}}</ref> Then, the Kodaira–Spencer map sends a deformation<blockquote><math>\frac{k[\varepsilon][x_1,\ldots, x_n]}{
f + \varepsilon g
} </math></blockquote>to the element <math>g \in \text{Ext}^1(\mathbf{L}_{X_0/k}, \mathcal{O}_{X_0}) </math>.
